source: OROS setting creator sources + OrosIdn.dll + a running NVGate
note: Catalogue of NVGate setting identifiers (IDNs), one record per setting. Each record carries both forms of the identifier: `idn_text` (`frontEnd.input3.label`, the modern form) and `idn_legacy` (`1.3.1`, still accepted and used by older programs). `module`, `submodule` and `setting` are the three parts of `idn_text`, split for convenience. `name` is the label NVGate shows for that setting in the Analyzer Setting Browser; it is null where the setting could not be queried because its plug-in was inactive when this file was produced. `type` tells you how to format the value you send. Where NVGate has no text name for a component, that component keeps its number: a submodule becomes a number and an index (`dynamicOperating.674:1.label`), a setting keeps its number (`dynamicOperating.channel1.447`). Those identifiers are just as valid - both forms were checked against a running analyzer - only less readable, which is what `name` is for. Settings that are never exposed to users are not listed at all. **A submodule ending in a number is one member of a numbered family**: the catalogue lists `frontEnd.input1`, and `frontEnd.input3.label` addresses the third input in exactly the same way - only the number changes. How many members exist depends on your hardware and licence, so ask the analyzer rather than assume: `GetSubModuleList frontEnd.input1` returns the full list. The same holds for `fft1.channel1`, `recorder.track1` and every other numbered collection. `setting_name_aliases` in this header lists the few settings that accept a second spelling: `frontEnd.input1.name` works as well as `frontEnd.input1.label`. Older code often uses the alternative. To confirm anything here, press Shift + right-click on the setting in NVGate: it shows both forms of its identifier.
